extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of scientific method, philosophers of science, and scientific inquirers
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for evaluating hypotheses, empirical (derivative) laws, and progressive effects in scientific inquiry — when inductive vs deductive methods are appropriate and what limits apply to generalizations. Includes treatment of causation, composition of causes, and methods of proof (agreement/difference).

rubrics_metrics.name: Legitimate inductive inference about past causes
rubrics_metrics.description: Infer from an observed effect the existence, in time past, of a cause similar to that by which we know it to be produced in all cases in which we have actual experience of its origin.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the legitimate operation of inferring past events (e.g., geological inferences about rock deposits or judicial inferences from a corpse). Proceed when the agents and laws are known and uniformities are ascertained 'by a perfect induction without any mixture of hypothesis.' Examples: geology (inferring igneous origin from cooled matter), judicial inquiries (inferring murder from marks on a corpse). Avoid treating purely conjectural agencies as equivalent to such inductive inferences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish hypotheses from inductive conclusions
rubrics_metrics.description: Inventing agencies to account for classes of phenomena (hypotheses) is different from inferring past collocations of known agents in conformity with known laws (induction).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hypotheses may be 'probable conjecture, not a proved truth.' Use caution: hypotheses introduce suppositions (e.g., intervening mediums) and are not equivalent to conclusions drawn by strict induction. Do not conflate speculative agency-inventions with inductive demonstrations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer explanations using only known laws/substances
rubrics_metrics.description: Theories that introduce no unknown substances, properties, or laws and proceed from known laws are less hypothetical in character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Laplace’s nebular speculation is cited: because it invokes only known laws (cooling, conservation principles, gravitation) it 'participates essentially in the inductive character' of geology, though still weaker in evidence. Even such theories remain provisional because they assume the permanence of existing laws over long times.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proximate vs remote cause in progressive effects
rubrics_metrics.description: When an instantaneous cause produces a permanent (progressive) effect, each subsequent stage of the effect is proximately caused by the immediately preceding stage rather than by the original remote cause.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: a projectile’s later motion is caused by the previous instant’s motion (the 'force generated' by previous motion); when a resisting medium retards motion, subsequent states reflect the retarded (proximate) cause. For precise causal language, consider each link in a succession as effect of the link before it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat continuous causes as series of successive causes (composition of causes)
rubrics_metrics.description: A cause that continues in action should be analyzed as a succession of similar causes introduced successively; the total progressive effect is the sum of the separate effects each would produce.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rusting of iron or continued gravitational action are examples: progressive rusting is the sum of many successive particle actions; continued gravity is equivalent to series of forces generating incremental motion. This viewpoint justifies mathematical/deductive treatment of such accumulations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use deductive/mathematical methods for infinitesimal progressive accumulation
rubrics_metrics.description: When continuance of a cause adds fixed increments (equal quantities in equal times), the result can and should be computed by mathematical/deductive principles (differential calculus).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Problems asking what effect results from continual addition of a given cause, or how much of a cause produces a given effect, are mathematical. Such cases are especially suited to deductive treatment rather than experimental investigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for progressive change in the cause itself
rubrics_metrics.description: If a permanent cause also undergoes progressive change in circumstances that determine the effect, the resulting effect combines accumulation and change and will not be a simple equal-increment series.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: seasonal temperature rise is due to both the continuance of solar heating and the progressive change in solar position/day length. Model both components (accumulation + progressive change) when predicting effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize interaction and feedback between causes and effects (periodicity)
rubrics_metrics.description: In systems where effects react upon causes, the causes at each instant may be altered by previous effects, potentially producing periodic or non-periodic outcomes depending on initial ratios.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Planetary motion: central attraction and acquired motion interact, and the reaction of motion upon the causes can render the system periodic (elliptical) or non-returning (parabolic/hyperbolic) depending on ratios. Analyze potential feedbacks and initial conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical law defined as derivative, provisional regularity
rubrics_metrics.description: Empirical laws are observed uniformities on which we hesitate to rely beyond observed cases because we do not see the reason why such laws should hold; they are derivative laws awaiting resolution into simpler laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: local tidal laws, weather sequences, certain chemical/biological tendencies. The ascertainment of empirical laws often precedes their deductive explanation; verification of deductions often compares with previously observed empirical laws.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit empirical laws to observed time/place/circumstance
rubrics_metrics.description: Empirical laws can only be received as true within the limits of time, place, and circumstance in which they have been found true by observation; they should not be extended beyond those limits without trial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because derivative laws may depend on collocations (arrangements) of causes, which are not governed by a law, an empirical law true on Earth (e.g., coal-bed superposition) cannot be assumed true on other planets. Exercise restraint in generalization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish derivative laws from laws vs collocations
rubrics_metrics.description: A derivative law may result from ultimate laws alone, or from ultimate laws plus a particular collocation (arrangement) of causes; if the latter, it cannot be reduced to law and lacks universal necessity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investigate whether a uniformity arises from single-cause effects (likely resolvable into laws) or from combined effects of several causes (may depend on collocations). The presence of collocation undermines universal extension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method of Agreement alone insufficient to establish causes
rubrics_metrics.description: When the only proof for a generalization is the Method of Agreement (observing common circumstances across cases), the generalization amounts to an empirical law, not an ultimate law of causation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Method of Agreement can identify aggregates of common circumstances but cannot determine which are true causes versus collateral or coexisting effects. To establish causation, supplement agreement with Method of Difference or deductive explanation ('a priori' account).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid inferring causation from uniform succession of stages
rubrics_metrics.description: Uniform succession (e.g., seedling to tree, spring to summer) does not by itself mean one stage causes the next; both may be successive effects of a common cause.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not call an earlier stage the cause of a later one merely because of gradual resemblance and succession; seek the underlying continuing processes (nutrition, sap rise, etc.) and verify by induction/experiment whether those processes account for the growth as accumulated effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical inference requires established uniformities without hypothesis
rubrics_metrics.description: In enquiring into past events (geology, forensics), inferential claims are legitimate when they proceed 'in conformity with known laws' and on uniformities ascertained by induction 'without any mixture of hypothesis.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the judicial analogy: as in determining cause of death from the corpse, rely on uniformities established by prior strict induction. If agents are not directly known to have been present, proceed when no other known cause could have generated the observed effects.
